body.text: When discussions turn to Australia’s artificial intelligence future, the debate quickly becomes one of technological sovereignty. Should Australia build its own frontier AI models? Is reliance on American technology companies a strategic vulnerability? Can Australia ever become self-sufficient in AI?
These are important questions. But they risk focusing attention on the wrong problem.

Australia’s greatest AI vulnerability is not dependence on foreign technologies. It is the risk of becoming dependent on others for the capabilities needed to adopt, integrate, govern and continually improve those technologies. Avoiding that dependence demands, for example, certain workforce skills and an expert regulatory capability. ‘AI readiness’ may be the best term for describing the result of such preparations.

No country, not even the United States, controls every critical technology. Modern innovation depends on international collaboration, global supply chains and specialised expertise spread across multiple countries. Even the world’s largest technology firms rely on semiconductor manufacturing in Taiwan, lithography equipment from the Netherlands, specialised materials from Japan, and research talent drawn globally.
Nonetheless, a country can and should aim for self-reliance in the latter part of the chain, with AI readiness.

A country may import AI models while retaining deep domestic skill in applying them. Equally, it may possess access to the world’s best technologies yet lack the expertise, institutions and industrial capacity needed to translate those technologies into economic and strategic advantage. That is Australia’s real challenge.

Australia necessarily accesses many of the world’s most advanced AI systems through trusted partners. The question is whether it possesses the capability to integrate AI into defence, critical infrastructure, public administration, healthcare, education and industry faster and more effectively than its competitors.
Owning technology is only one source of strategic advantage. Knowing how to deploy it at scale is another.

History repeatedly demonstrates this distinction. Many countries have imported advanced military equipment. And many of them have failed to develop the doctrine, logistics, industrial base, workforce and organisational capability needed to use those systems effectively.

Artificial intelligence presents a similar challenge. Buying an. AI service will not automatically increase national productivity or strengthen defence capability. Success, achieving AI readiness, depends on complementary investments in data infrastructure, cyber security, digital skills, organisational redesign, governance, regulatory capability and continuous learning.
These things cannot be imported; they must be developed.

Current discussions often frame AI as a race to build domestic models or establish national technology champions. Those ambitions may deliver rewards, but they should not become the primary measure of Australia’s AI success.

Australia’s comparative advantage has rarely come from attempting to replicate the industrial strengths of much larger economies. Instead, it has consistently depended on combining domestic expertise with trusted international partnerships. The same logic should guide AI strategy.

Australia does not need to produce every critical technology domestically. But it needs to keep a national ability to evaluate, adopt, adapt, govern and, where necessary, independently operate technologies that originate elsewhere.
That requires long-term investment in people as much as technology.

Universities, vocational education, digital infrastructure, public sector capability, defence innovation, cyber resilience and research institutions must be treated as strategic assets rather than simply as economic investments. Stronger connections between government, universities, industry and defence must also be built so that knowledge moves rapidly across sectors.
However, capability cannot be built in isolation. Nor should Australia think about AI readiness purely in national terms.

Trusted international partnerships remain essential. Cooperation with the US, Japan, South Korea, India, Singapore and European partners will continue to shape Australia’s technological future. But partnerships are most valuable when they strengthen Australia’s domestic capability rather than substitute for it.

In an era of strategic competition, resilience depends less on owning every technology than on possessing the capability to use technologies effectively, adapt to future innovations and recover quickly when disruption occurs.
That is ultimately what national power increasingly requires.

The AI debate should therefore move beyond a narrow discussion of technological dependence. The more important question is whether Australia is building the readiness that will allow it to remain strategically autonomous in a world where technological interdependence is inevitable.
Technology will continue to evolve. AI readiness is what will allow Australia to keep pace.
